answers: Dinosaurs may have been much more like modern birds than we knew—and not just because some had feathers. A new study suggests that mighty dinosaurs of yore didn't roar, contrary to every dinosaur movie you've ever seen. Instead, they made a decidedly less scary sound called a "closed-mouth vocalization." Think of a dove cooing or perhaps an ostrich doing this grunting thing. As the scientists explain in the journal Evolution, per UT News, the sound actually comes out of the neck area after air is pushed through an esophageal pouch. In fact, the animal's mouth is shut the whole time. Lots of birds do this today, and because birds descended from dinosaurs, scientists suspect they may have communicated in a similar way. The fossil record can't prove it, though the Washington Post notes that previous research meshes with the idea, including the belief that dinosaurs had air sacs instead of vocal chords. “A cool thing about this work is the demonstration that closed-mouth behavior evolved many times,” says the lead author. “That suggests it can emerge fairly easily and be incorporated into mating displays" among different types of animals. A co-author says the study gives the impression of "a very different Jurassic world. Not only were dinosaurs feathered, but they may have had bulging necks and made booming, closed-mouth sounds." But if so, the makers of Jurassic Park didn't get it all wrong: The hiss of the film's velociraptors came from a goose, per Vulture. (Scientists have grown chickens with dinosaur legs.)

Recent scientific research has challenged long-standing portrayals of dinosaurs, particularly the Tyrannosaurus rex, in popular media. Traditionally depicted as roaring monsters, dinosaurs may have sounded quite different. New studies suggest that some dinosaurs, especially large-bodied ones, may have produced low, throaty sounds similar to modern birds, such as pigeons or ostriches, rather than the dramatic roars often heard in movies like *Jurassic Park*.

The research, published in the journal *Evolution*, analyzed the vocal behaviors of living birds and crocodiles, which are part of the archosaur group that includes dinosaurs. Scientists found that closed-mouth vocalizations—sounds produced without opening the beak—are more common in larger birds, such as doves, ostriches, and cassowaries. These sounds are generated by air passing through an esophageal pouch, creating low-frequency, resonant noises. This type of vocalization is typically used in mating or territorial displays.

The study suggests that closed-mouth vocalizations evolved independently in multiple lineages, including birds, crocodiles, and possibly non-avian dinosaurs. Since many dinosaurs were large-bodied, it is likely that some of them used similar vocal techniques. However, direct fossil evidence of dinosaur sounds is scarce, as soft tissues like vocal organs do not fossilize well.

The research also highlights the creative process behind the sounds in *Jurassic Park*. Sound designer Gary Rydstrom used a variety of animal sounds—such as tortoises, geese, horses, and even a Jack Russell terrier—to create the iconic dinosaur noises. While the T. rex roar was based on a baby elephant’s cry, other sounds, like those of velociraptors, were inspired by birds and other animals.

Despite these insights, much about dinosaur vocalizations remains a mystery. Scientists continue to explore how dinosaurs might have sounded by combining fossil data, experimental physiology, and sound modeling. The findings not only reshape our understanding of dinosaur behavior but also suggest that the Jurassic world was more complex and nuanced than previously imagined, with dinosaurs possibly having feathers, bulging necks, and a range of vocalizations that were more bird-like than monstrous.
